strengths: This work introduces an approach to extract pseudo-tactile information from vision and contact locations for robotic grasping tasks. The topic is interesting, the pipeline is presented with details, and the experiment results show the effectiveness of the approach with high accuracy.
Open-sourced dataset of point cloud images is made available.
The work has clear writing and good structure which makes it easy to follow and understand.
It is well-motivated to address the hard-to-acquire tactile perception by using vision for dexterous robotic hands.
The authors provide abundunt and clear explanation for method presentation, and present a simple yet effective approach for point cloud preprocessing and feature extraction.
The authors give a thorough representation on the expermental setup, and conduct real-world experiments on a dexterous hand for validation.
The result of the experiments seems very ideal, indicating the effectiveness of the proposed method.
weaknesses: The vision-based "pseudo tactile" features are derived using some common tools for point cloud data processing.
The simulation for finger tip localization is from replicating and transforming the real motion data into the simulated environment.
It is claimed that the combination of this vision-based information and the fingertip contact points can enhance tactile feedback reliability in robotic grasping, but this is not clear.
The experiment does not show how the robotic grasping is improved.
Paper repeatedly talks about the "Y component of the normal vector" without clearly defining a coordinate frame.
Authors mention employing "policy fine-tuning techniques" on page 7 without ever mentioning a policy up until this point.

The role of simulation in the paper is not clear; the described real-time linkage sounds like a simple forward kinematics problem that would only require a mathematical model of the robot, not a full-fledged simulation.
Paper claims that Intel RealSense has "sub-mm accuracy", which is not supported by documentation from the manufacturer.

Section 4.2 claims to assess localization precision, but it is unclear what the ground truth is, how this is being measured, and what measurement is being compared against this ground truth; Table 4 is difficult to understand and has no mention of errors or comparative ground truth.
An RMSE error is reported with no clarity on what quantities are being compared.

It is unclear how related work Section 2.3 is connected to this work; pseudo-haptics is associated with giving humans touch sensory feedback, whereas "pseudo-tactile" in this paper is related to analyzing the surface tactile properties of objects.
The paper is very poorly formatted; main result tables are placed in the appendix and are difficult to understand.

Results in Tables 4, 5, and 6 have a poor choice of units (meters when dealing with textures that are likely sub‑cm scale) and numbers are represented with arbitrary precision without regard for the precision and error rates of the depth measurement device.
I do not think this work has solid contribution or concrete experimental results.

The proposed method simply combines existing techniques such as extracting point cloud from RGBD camera and using a simulator to simulate grasping; the work should be extended to more dynamic manipulation tasks and explore whether the extracted object features can be leveraged for these complicated tasks.

The paper lacks novelty because many parts of the method chapter are biased towards engineering practice rather than innovation; point cloud preprocessing, camera coordinate system transformations, and similar work are common in robotics, and the texture extraction method overlaps with [1].
The authors did not measure how good the quality of the generated pseudo-haptic signals were, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

The experiments are inadequate and lack comparison with previous work; there are no baselines for contact position localization, no ablation studies on aspects such as KDTree radius or normal threshold, etc.
